content: Yahya pursued spatial control through modern means: ﬁscal centralisation, military modernisation and bureaucratic organisation. Yet more than the formation of a modern state, the Imam Yahya’s country, led by the imam, is a ‘new state space which was organised according to hierarchies of religious knowledge’ (118). The new northern regime embraced a trans-local Muslim brotherhood, distancing itself from the inherent divisiveness of European nation-state systems. Nonetheless, this Pan-Islamic disciplin- ing of space collapsed as border skirmishes occurred between two Muslim countries, Yemen and Saudi Arabia. On the southern border, British aerial bombardments also impeded the expansion of Imam Yahya’s Islamic domain. Yet aside from the rich and dense histories crystallised by Unmaking North and South, readers seldom catch a glimpse of the nation. Willis admits that the major nationalist discourse emerged after 1934, yet it is a history that falls outside the range of the book. He uncovers that the supposedly timeless and placeless nation was absent in the pre-1934 era. Instead of imaging a linear, teleological path of the national body, what this important book successfully reanimates is a compounded history, one that simultaneously unfolded with colonial envisioning of the tribal landscapes and with the Islamic production of moral spaces. The illustrative depictions of the historical geographies cements this book as a reading of spatial history. And by showing competing spatial disciplines, Willis’ account also provides a vivid picture of modes of political belonging in Yemen. Albeit without investigating familiar factors underpinning the nation, a reason for national- ism scholars to pay attention is the book’s central theme: it denaturalises the nation to the contingent. And unexpectedly, by avoiding discussion of the nation, Unmaking North and South in the end successfully locates the nation in place and in time. SU HU University of Edinburgh Cynthia Cockburn, Anti-militarism: Political and Gender Dynamics of Peace Move- ments. Great Britain: Palgrave Macmillan, 2012, 297pp. Writing is therapeutic. At some level, she put words in a row to make sense of themselves, their world, or both together. Cynthia Cockburn’s Anti-militarism, with its ironic volley subtitle of Political and Gender Dynamics of Peace Movements, sharpens and deepens the critique with which she has persistently confronted audiences across the world. The book is organised in nine parts. In chapter one the book examines three moments in the life of the British peace movement and she ask wonderful question on what was going to just then in national and international politics, and in relations between women and men, femininity and masculinity? The periods on which she focuses are the decades following the Napoleonic wars that ended in 1815; the years that span the Great wars of 1914–1918; and the early 1980s, when US nuclear missiles were bunkered in British bases. Chapter two deals with entire movement within the bounds of one network, a supportive framework for those, worldwide, who refuse obligatory service in the military? More than that, however, it is a movement against armies and war-ﬁghting, and for a just social and economic order. Two major 590 Book Reviews © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

contradictions have been a source of intense debate within WRI over its ninety-year history. The ﬁrst lies in the difﬁculty of pursuing a struggle that is both effective and principled-achieving economic and social revolutionary change by means of nonviolent direct action. The second has to do with gender. She also curiously followed war resistance to Spain, to look in some detail at one of WRI’s associate organisations, the Alternativa Anti-militarista: Movimiento de Objeccion de Conciencia, and its civil disobedience against the militarism of the Spanish state. Chapter three tells the story of how, for twenty-ﬁve years, every move the state made to corral its young men into military service was met by the objectors with a strategy of refusal, dramatising their paciﬁsm and embarrassing the authorities. AA-MOC shares with other social move- ments (of greens, squatters, neighborhoods, women) a pre-ﬁgurative methodology (nonviolence, horizontal organising) that differentiates all of them from the traditional left. Women joined the movement ﬁrst as family and friends supporting male objectors, then as activists making feminist sense of militarism. While some persisted in dual militancy in the male-dominated movement, others left to start Women in Black, a network not only against war but against aggression against women. While chapter four takes a single city, Leicester in the English Midlands, at a speciﬁc moment, the Israeli assault on the Palestinian territory of Gaza between 27 December 2008 and 18 January 2009, and ask who these people were that came out to stand together in the town center and call for peace and justice. The case reveals some of the difﬁculties and rewards of negotiating a contingent local alliance between profoundly divergent cultures and ideologies. And chapter ﬁve describes the mobilisation, the political diversity of the participating organisations, and the threaten reaction of the authorities. She reﬂects on an initiative in which She shared to bring women to Stras- bourg to join the demonstration and contribute a ‘feminist case against NATO’. A key theme in the chapter is violence – the violence of the state security forces and the violence of some demonstrators – which raised questions concerning the scope and methods of our movement. In chapter six, Naoko Ikedia and Cynthia Cockburn address the Japanse anti-war/anti-militarist/peace movement, which they found to be markedly divided between socialist and communist streams. They devoted particular attention to Okinawa, islands whose people suffer under both Japanese economic and ethnic hegemony and an overbearing US military presence. Looking at chapter seven the tendency in South Korea’s reuniﬁcation movement to an emphasis on nationhood, and its tolerance of the North’s nuclear strategy, distance it from an anti-militarist movement that seeks the disarming of the peninsula and the removal of US forces from the region. Some organisations, however, seek to participate constructively in movements, working toward a peace culture in everyday life, and elaborating the creative project of a democratic ‘peace state’ encompassing both Koreas. Chapter eight and nine presented the ﬁnal case study of another network, the International Action Network on Small Arms (IANSA). IANSA is a transitional advocacy network that lobbies international agencies and state governments for imple- mentation of a programme of action for the worldwide control of manufacture, export, sale, ownership and use of small arms and light weapons. And drawing together the insights she gained from the preceding studies, she analyses some thoughts about anti-war, anti-militarist and peace activism as a social movement, a global movement of many parts. Importantly, it provides some excellent case studies such as the IANSA and the Japanse anti-war/anti-militarist/peace movement. In all cases, Cynthia Cockburn and Naoko Ikedia provide important lessons and observations, as well as interesting Book Reviews 591 © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

statistics. This book serves as a critical ontological tool in several ﬁelds of scholarly analysis, casting analytic light upon the contentious ground that the very practice of war is regulated so artiﬁcially as to ascribe allegedly and profoundly immoral and unethical advantages to those conducting it. Although this is a determined and praise- worthy endeavor, Cynthia Cockburn’s work suffers from certain theoretical and sub- stantive limitations, but not to an extent that its contribution to its ﬁelds of discourse might diminish considerably. In sum, the book is an excellent scholarly work dealing with anti-militarism in the context of Political and Gender Dynamics of Peace Movements events. The chapters, as already noted, are well written and researched. The book includes an extensive, detailed list of references provides the reader with an excellent starting point for further examination, if desired. OLUWASEUN BAMIDELE Faith Academy Daron Acemoglu and James A. Robinson, Why Nations Fail: the Origins of Power, Prosperity, and Poverty. New York, Crown Business, 2012, 529pp. $17.00 (pbk). Why Nations Fail is an ambitious interdisciplinary theorisation of global economic inequality. Its starting point is the striking example of Nogales. The city is bisected by a fence. Its prosperous northern half is located in Arizona, its poorer southern half in Sonora, Mexico. Acemoglu, an economist at MIT, and Robinson, a Harvard political scientist, contend that the border itself is the explanation for this disparity. They hold that the Nogales example contradicts two seriously misleading but per- sistent analyses of economic development. The ﬁrst of these is the geography hypoth- esis, which explains poverty and wealth by reference to latitude: temperate climates have an economic advantage over tropical or semi-tropical ones. Jeffrey Sachs, for example, in The End of Poverty (2006), argues that tropical diseases lower labour productivity, and that tropical soil quality suppresses agricultural output. Yet there is no geographical variation between the two halves of Nogales, and Singapore, Malay- sia, and Botswana also contradict the geography hypothesis. The second theory rejected by the authors is the culture hypothesis, according to which religious values, social norms and ethics constitute the primary determi- nants of economic success or failure. The most famous example of the culture hypothesis remains Weber’s The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905). Acemoglu and Robinson concede that modern capitalism originated in the Protestant countries of England and the Netherlands, but they also point out that capitalist economic practices were rapidly assimilated by Catholic France. And the more recent economic successes in East Asia clearly owe nothing to any form of Christianity. Returning to Nogales, there are minor cultural differences north and south of the border, particularly as they relate to the economically signiﬁcant factor of trust. But these differences are too small to explain the wealth gap and they are, the authors contend, the products of antecedent differences in American and Mexican institutions. 592 Book Reviews © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

The thesis of the book – unmistakable because so very often repeated throughout – is that a country’s degree of economic success is determined primarily by the character of its institutions: poor countries are poor because they have mutually-reinforcing extractive economic and political institutions, whereas rich countries have mutually- reinforcing inclusive ones. Extractive economic institutions have three characteristics: they extract resources from the general population for the beneﬁt of a ruling elite; they fail to protect property rights; and they deny incentives for economic activity. Inclusive economic institutions are simply the binary opposite: they provide open markets; they guarantee property rights; and they enable people to beneﬁt from their own economic endeavours. Both extractive and inclusive economic institutions create their own corresponding political institutions. The authors concede that there are two ways in which economic growth can be achieved under extractive institutions. Firstly, elites can coercively allocate resources to those high-productivity economic activities that they control. Examples include the use of slaves by the planter elite in the production of Caribbean sugar for world markets in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, or the state’s forced redeployment of labour from agriculture to industry in the Soviet Five Year Plans. Secondly, the controlled and limited introduction of inclusive economic institutions can also create growth, as in South Korea under its military dictatorship, or the economic reforms in post-Maoist China. But the authors insist that economic growth under extractive institutions cannot be maintained over time. This is because extractive institutions serve the interests of established elites, whereas a prerequisite of economic growth is ‘creative destruction’ – Schumpeter’s term for the process by which economic innovation inevitably threatens existing economic practices and those who beneﬁt from them. ‘The solution to the economic and political failure of nations today’, Acemoglu and Robinson conclude, ‘is to transform their extractive institutions towards inclusive ones’ (402). Why Nations Fail does not have a recipe for economic development, but it suggests the ingredients necessary for the achievement of inclusive institutions: sufﬁ- cient centralisation to prevent challenges to extractive institutions from degenerating into disorder, pre-existing political institutions that accommodate pluralism, and a viable civil society. There is no Whig teleology, or sociological modernisation theory, in this argument. The impediments to achieving inclusive institutions are considered at length, and Robert Michels’ ‘iron law of oligarchy’ is invoked to explain, for example, the per- petuation of extractive institutions in the postcolonial world, or the failure so far of the 2011 Egyptian Revolution. But two important realities are omitted from this quintessentially liberal argument. Firstly, the book rightly details the brutality of extractive institutions, but the history of inclusive institutions has its dark side too: were the immediate human consequences of the enclosure movement in early modern England, or of Manifest Destiny in nineteenth-century North America, justiﬁed by the rationalisation of property rights? Secondly, the authors take no account of radical perspectives in which military- industrial complexes, and ﬁnancial bailouts, make developed world institutions appear extractive. PETER C. GROSVENOR Paciﬁc Lutheran University Book Reviews 593 © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

Harris Mylonas, The Politics of Nation-Building: Making Co-Nationals, Refugees, and Minorities. Cambridge, UK: Cambridge University Press, 2012, 273pp. £53.95 (hbk). The Politics of Nation-Building is a powerful new book bound to leave its mark on nationalism studies. It combines original thinking with competent execution, and manages to appeal to a readership beyond disciplinary, theoretical and methodological boundaries. In the context of turn of the nineteenth century Balkan politics, the book charts the international dynamics behind various nation-building policies in the region; but the argument is a generalisable one applicable across time and place. The new nation-states arising from the ashes of multi-ethnic, multi-faith, imperial territories of the Ottomans all differed on how they pursued national consolidation after independ- ence. Put simply, this is a book that prioritises the geostrategic element behind elite policy choices in these nation-building projects. Harris Mylonas relies on both quan- titative and archival evidence in his investigation of the reasons behind the policies of accommodation, assimilation, or exclusion towards the non-core ethnic groups resi- dent in the new nation-states. His geostrategic argument connects the domestic and the international levels of analysis in a parsimonious way, but there is also a fair shade of nuance in how factors from the two level interact, so it is best to quote Mylonas himself: A non-core group supported by an enemy external power and residing in a revisionist host state is more likely to be excluded than targeted with assimilation or accommo- dation; if a similar group were to reside in a status quo state, it would most likely be targeted with assimilationist policies; taking the form of colonisation by core group members and internal displacement of non-core group members. Finally, non-core groups supported by allied states are more likely to be accommodated than be assimi- lated or excluded (48). Mylonas’ account of that time-period is thoughtful and rigorous, and he examines the subject through various angles. In due course, The Politics of Nation-Building offers not only substantive and theoretical lessons, but also guidelines for methodological improvements (as well as policy advice). Some of the methodological practices in mainstream social science receive gentle but learned criticisms from the author; and this never feels like Mylonas is on his soapbox on the margins of mainstream social science questioning the entire establishment. In fact, this is why The Politics of Nation-Building deserves to be part of nationalism studies canon: it does not read like theoretical/ methodological partisan book, but is driven by a desire to understand and explain the political patterns deﬁning nation-building. The intellectual courage to question the artiﬁcially neat categories and decontextualised analyses deﬁning contemporary social sciences; and yet does this in a language and theoretical/methodological repertoire accessible to all analytical schools. It is, however, the strength of the argument that remains the main contribution of the book. The contemporary lesson that Mylonas instils from the new nation-states that replaced the Ottomans is quite clear: neighbours matter in how state elites view their minorities. That being said, what has to be added to the picture Mylonas paints is the massive displacements and political changes accompanying the dismemberment of the Ottoman Empire, creating local power vacuums and uncertainty. As the empire’s territories shrunk with unprecedented speed, hundreds of thousands of the wrong ethnicity/ religion were cleansed from the new nation-states; those who found themselves on wrong sides of the new borders reinvented their ethnic/religious roots; refugees were 594 Book Reviews © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

resented by the locals; new states were born without a full cadre of bureaucrats, judges, prosecutors, and police; militias became liberators but could not immediately deliver on law and order; lines of communication between various imperial territories were cut; bandits roamed the countryside and beneﬁtted from the chaos; countless soldiers and civilians died from disease and hunger; and all of this happened during the course of a few decades. Such whirlwind of change and displacement does not always make for purposive and coherent policy-making. Moreover, during the course of all this, many younger Ottoman ofﬁcers were replacing the legitimising discourse of a multi-ethnic, multi-faith Empire and adopting a new Turkish national project while more conservative elements close to the sublime Porte were embracing Islamism as the new legitimising discourse, and court elites from non-core groups kept their attachment to a lingering Ottomanism. In other words, the Ottoman elites were not a coherent lot during the decades of change Mylonas examines. Similar divisions existed among the elites of the new nation-states as well – often divided into radical nationalist revolutionaries and conservative cultural/religious nationalists. The changing demographic and geographic dynamics in the region as well as inconsistencies at the top signal the need to turn assumptions of purposive and coherent policy-making by state elites a notch down. But at the end of the day, this is but a minor issue in an otherwise masterly volume. JAN ERK Leiden University Sigal R. Ben-Porath and Rogers M. Smith, Varieties of Sovereignty and Citizenship. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 2013, 352pp. £52.00 (hbk). This valuable book, like many edited, multi-author works, has both ﬁne points and ﬂaws. It is an interdisciplinary volume, the product of an initiative sponsored by the Penn Program on Democracy, Citizenship, and Constitutionalism in 2009–2010. Its diverse set of contributors includes philosophers and normative political theorists, social scientists, legal scholars and even an analyst of rhetoric. The book assumes the nation-state’s power is diminishing and considers implications of this change. As it does so, it considers how important phenomena such as war, immigration, sovereignty, and citizenship may be intertwined in the early twenty-ﬁrst century, focusing on three main themes: differences in military action and its consequences; transnational migration and the changing strategies of states in dealing with migrant populations; and theories that the Westphalian order is giving way or should give way to ‘cosmopolitanism’. The book combines empirical/descriptive and normative modes of inquiry as it engages these issues. Chapters organised into three sections follow a clearly written introduction by the editors. The ﬁrst section, called ‘War, Sovereignty, and Plural Citizenships’, seems to have as its main goal understanding some of the empirical issues at the nexus both inter and intra-state conﬂict and citizenship. The four chapters included in this section are consistently interesting, but relate to each other only vaguely. Arjun Chowdhury offers theoretical musings about the relationship between states, empires, and state systems. His core, and indeed useful, observation is that the ‘state system’ has always been Book Reviews 595 © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

somewhat unstable and prone to crisis, with many more ‘failures’ than we tend to remember. This is followed by a chapter from Sidney Tarrow that attempts to discern which is more predictive: Laswell’s theory that war leads to an anti-democratic ‘garri- son state’ or Tilly’s theory that inter-state, total wars led to both the rise of the modern state and, under certain conditions, to its democratic variant. The chapter is inconclu- sive, generating numerous plausible but as of yet untested hypotheses. Anna Tsing reports poignantly on some lived consequences of proxy wars. Nasser Hussain analyses counterinsurgency, treating it ‘as a discourse of sovereignty and a discourse of empire’ (76). The second section is entitled ‘Immigration, Sovereignty, and Plural Citizenships’. It begins with a cogent chapter by Peter Schuck on the difﬁculties faced by the United States in countering the threat of ‘citizen terrorists’ after the rise of plural citizenship. This is followed by Michael Blake’s nuanced consideration of the ethical obligations a state may or may not take on vis-à-vis potential or actual immigrants by virtue of either (a) creating the conditions that engender a need for safe harbor or (b) through becom- ing systematically dependent on a migrant population of non-citizens. The section is closed by Ayelet Shachar’s thoughtful chapter on ‘rootedness’, which proposes a novel, intriguing, normative basis for the acquisition of citizenship. The third and ﬁnal section is entitled ‘On Cosmopolitan Alternatives’. It contains six chapters that center on arguments for and against national and cosmopolitan forms of identity and politics. This section reads as a kind of book within a book, and is somewhat more tightly focused than the preceding sections. Robert Goodin argues that an incipient global government is already with us, and that this is a good thing. Jeremy Rabkin provides a strident critique of cosmopolitanism. Pheng Cheah writes opaquely about cosmopolitanism’s ‘physico-material bases’. Elizabeth Povinelli asks challenging questions about the cultural biases of existing cosmopoli- tan visions, drawing on ‘critical indigenous theory’. David Miller proposes that citi- zenship is necessarily political and that much of what is called ‘global citizenship’ amounts, therefore, to nothing but a ‘ghostly shadow’ (227). Anna Stilz closes the book with a particularly strong chapter on the role of the state in our political and moral obligations. As a whole, this interesting volume has mixed success in achieving its objectives. Its contribution to empirical work on the state, sovereignty and citizenship is limited. As noted above, each of the more empirical essays does have something to offer. Taken together, though, they produce no clear picture, but rather a sense of analytical discord: each is linked to arguments taking place in different literatures and pitched at different levels. The more normatively oriented chapters – despite often begging major questions in the empirical generalisations they make – achieve greater convergence around clear themes, and the disagreements between their authors are therefore more productive, even if their ultimate resolution seems unlikely. Given the quality of many of the individual contributions, though, and the insights that emerge at various points throughout the book, many scholars interested in questions of political identity, citi- zenship, sovereignty, and related themes will want to have it on their shelves. In short, this journal’s audience will likely ﬁnd Varieties of Sovereignty and Citizenship well worth reading. JONATHAN EASTWOOD Washington and Lee University 596 Book Reviews © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

Feargal Cochrane, Northern Ireland: The Reluctant Peace. London: Yale University Press, 2013, 352pp. £21.25 (hbk). As the title of this book implies, the lack of consensus between rival unionist, loyalist, and Irish nationalist groups means that the ‘peace process’ in Northern Ireland cannot be considered complete. Cochrane perceptively describes the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement of 1998 as simply an ‘agreement to disagree’ over the past, present, and future of the territory, and he examines the rival identities that are present within Northern Ireland in terms of their antecedents and their current political aims and attitudes. The Belfast Agreement is discussed in its political, sociological and historical contexts. The text consists of three sections: the ﬁrst discusses the history of Northern Ireland prior to the Belfast Agreement. The second examines the processes through which the Agreement was reached, and the third analyses the political and cultural effects of the Agreement on contemporary Northern Irish society. One of the key contributions made in the text is to provide much-needed discussion of the contemporary situation; a postscript discusses the rioting that occurred after the decision taken (in December 2012) by Belfast City Council to reduce the number of days that the Union ﬂag ﬂies over City Hall. The violent response of the loyalist community to this decision is taken as evidence of the author’s core thesis; the peace in Northern Ireland is extremely fragile, and the territory remains wracked by sectarianism. Cochrane argues that despite the progress made in recent years, it would be unwise to exaggerate the extent to which Northern Ireland has a shared society or a sense of a shared future. The Belfast Agreement cemented rather than resolved a situation in which the cultural and political afﬁliations of Northern Irish commu- nities are strongly opposed. The author points out that despite the overly optimistic analyses of some academic and media commentators, sectarian attitudes remain stubbornly undiminished in the territory. Taking the existence of the devolved par- liament as conclusive evidence of a shared society is misguided, argues Cochrane; Northern Irish society remains fundamentally divided, with communities living in strictly demarcated areas and having different attitudes towards the ‘peace process’. Unionists and loyalists are increasingly disenchanted by the ‘concessions’ made to the Irish nationalist community, which by contrast remains broadly in favour of the process, as nationalist political parties are no longer excluded by discriminatory practices. Another principal argument is that there is a growing gap between the rhetoric of politicians and their actual desire and ability to create cross-community policies. Sinn Fein and the Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) have become the largest two parties in Northern Ireland, and they wish to ensure that this remains the case. Both are unwilling to promote initiatives that may be seen negatively in the communities that provide their core support. While there is less open hostility than at the height of the ‘Troubles’, political parties nevertheless focus only on creating legislation that beneﬁts their com- munity. Cochrane also discusses the signiﬁcance of civil society, and suggests that progress has been made through informal contributions to the peace process that could not have been made through the formal political sphere. This examination of the contribution of NGOs and non-afﬁliated individuals provides a very useful level of analysis, which is lacking in texts that focus solely on the actions of political parties and their leaders. The arguments contained within the text are generally consistent and persuasive, although there are some anomalies in the chapters that focus upon the con- temporary situation. Cochrane provides an extensive discussion of the threat posed to the peace process by dissident republicans, and this is persuasive. However, he then dismisses the potential of dissident groups such as the Real IRA to disrupt a process that he generally argues is very fragile. This seems unusual and is perhaps a consequence of writing about a constantly changing situation. The assessment of the genuine capacity of loyalists to disrupt the peace process is more consistent, however, and is brought into sharp relief by the post-script to the text. Northern Ireland: The Reluctant Peace would be of use to scholars looking for an insightful and non-partisan examination of the relationship between politics and culture in Northern Ireland. It would also be of interest to those looking for an analysis of the territory’s history. Cochrane’s arguments are made incisively and are generally persuasive. The depth of analysis contained within the text is one of its main strengths; providing the cultural background to the political process should be an essential element in all texts of this kind, but it is often overlooked. The author’s style is engaging and avoids jargon; personal anecdotes about the experience of growing up in Belfast during the Troubles are used sparingly but nevertheless provide an extra level of detail. The text is mainly of use to an academic audience, but is certainly accessible enough to appeal to a wider constituency. ANTHONY MAY Manchester Metropolitan University Marlene Laruelle and Sebastien Peyrouse, Globalising Central Asia: Geopolitics and the Challenges of Economic Development. London and New York: M. E. Sharpe 2013, 355pp. £29.50 (pbk). Some twenty years ago, the Soviet Central Asian republics of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan gained independence. The governments of these new states were confronted, virtually overnight and with almost no preparation, with a wide spectrum of internal and external problems. One of the most pressing issues was the need to transform economies that had been constituent parts of the larger Soviet economy, into viable national economies. Concomitantly, this required integration into the global economy. Meanwhile, foreign powers, large and small, vied with one another to gain access to the resources of these young states: a new era of ‘great games’ was born. This book deals with the complex process of establishing new networks and partnerships. It is divided into two parts. The ﬁrst part looks at the role of external players, devoting separate chapters to the ‘big four’ – Russia, United States, China and the European Union – then moves on to regional clusters in Asia and the Common- wealth of Independent States. The second part focuses on the main economic sectors, including agriculture (often neglected by other writers), hydrocarbons and minerals. 598 Book Reviews © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

The strength of this work is that it gives a clear, factual record of developments during this period, plentifully supplemented by statistical tables. It is somewhat weaker on analysis and contextualisation. In particular, there is little attempt to examine the dynamics of changing trends in the global economy and how this impacts on the Central Asian states. Thus, despite the careful listing of events, it is a curiously static account – things happen, but the pattern does not seem to change much. Yet this is a situation that is constantly evolving as new priorities, relation- ships and opportunities arise. If a book is to provide a deeper understanding of the subject it must be able to look at, but also beyond, current events. This is not to belittle the achievement of the authors. What they have done is valuable. It is not easy to amass such a quantity of information and to present it in accessible form. Rather, it is because the work is so good that it is possible to see what more could – and must eventually – be done. The beguiling title of the book poses, perhaps inadvertently, questions that are not really answered. The ‘challenges’ of economic development are many and varied, ranging from social disruption to environmental damage, but what are the chief issues of concern? And how, if at all, are they being addressed? On a conceptual level, is the term ‘globalising’ to be understood in a passive or an active sense? Is it a phenomenon that is imposed from outside, or are the Central Asian states part of the process, making choices, helping to shape the outcomes? The authors do not address this point directly, but the emphasis placed on external actors implicitly relegates these states to the role of hapless pawns. Of course there can be no denying the reality of power politics, but a more nuanced study would surely indicate that the Central Asian states have been rather skilful in steering their own courses, protecting their interests, deﬁning their goals and implementing their own agendas. A second question is whether or not ‘Central Asia’ can be regarded as a region. It is an amorphous space that can be mapped in a myriad of ways, depending on the choice of criteria. In recent usage, the term has gained currency as the collective designation for the ﬁve states (jokingly referred to as the ‘Stans’) that lie between Russia and China, the steppe and the Himalayan mountains. Certainly there are similarities, not least as a result of common experiences in the 20th century. Moreover, contiguity itself creates a degree of interaction. However, within this vast space there are many ﬁssures, ranging from socio-cultural attitudes to the natural environment – topography, resource endowment, levels of urbanisation and so forth. Features such as these have inﬂuenced the style and speed of development in each of these states. Since independence, diver- gence has been more evident than convergence. The authors note this tendency, but dismiss it briskly as ‘interstate failure’. That is too simplistic: the issues are complex and although they are resolvable (a process that is already underway), it will not be easy and is unlikely to be swift to achieve better cooperation. Yet until this happens, it is perhaps over optimistic to speak of ‘Central Asia’ as a region in anything but a purely geo- graphic sense. This is a stimulating work. It may not give as many answers as one might wish, but it does provide a sound basis for further discussion and research. It will undoubtedly be of interest to students, scholars and professional practitioners in a wide range of ﬁelds. SHIRIN AKINER University of Cambridge Book Reviews 599 © The author(s) 2014. Mark L. Haas, The Clash of Ideologies: Middle Eastern Politics and American Security. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2012, 302pp. £22.50 (pbk). How do ideologies shape international relations in general and America’s security interests in the Middle East in particular? This critical question is at the center of this book. Seeking to advance the theoretical debate in the international relations literature and provide policy guidance on key international security issues, Mark L. Haas argues that ‘the domestic dimension of leaders’ ideologies are likely to affect systematically their international choices in two broad ways’ (5). The ﬁrst way is the degree of ideological differences dividing leaders of any two ideological groups, what Haas calls ‘ideological distance’. The second way in which ideologies systematically shape leaders’ international policies is through the effects of the number of prominent ideological groups in any particular system, or what Haas calls ‘ideological polarity’. Ideological distance and ideological polarity are the two main causal variables in Haas’ model that are utilised to explain the change in leaders’ perception of threat and consequent security policies (the dependent variable). The Clash of Ideologies comprises ﬁve chapters. Chapter 1 lays out the book’s argument, and justiﬁes the case selection. The chapter begins with an explanation and assessment of ideological distance and ideological polarity, and how these two variables create security threats as well as opportunities in international relations. Contemporary multiple ideological groupings in the Middle East (e.g. Islamic fundamentalists, liber- als, and secular authoritarians) together with American interests in the region, make the selection of the four cases (Iran, Syria, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia) intellectually appealing. Placing the argument within the larger theoretical literature in international relations, Haas both complements and challenges major international relations theo- ries, including democratic peace, neorealism, and clash of civilisations. While the argument of this book is a strong challenge to the neorealist theory, and a complement to the democratic peace thesis, Haas is not predicting a ‘clash of civilizations,’ rather a ‘clash of ideologies.’ The subsequent chapters study the four cases. Chapter 2 examines the sources of Iranian enmity towards the United States, from 1997 to 2009. Dividing Iranian leaders into two groups (conservatives and reformers), Haas argues that ‘the huge ideological divide separating the United States from the Iranian conservatives pushed the latter to see America as both an inevitable threat to Iran’s security and a powerful force for domestic subversion’ (84). Iranian reformers, on the other hand, had a very different understanding of the nature of the threat posed by the United States and differed in how to address it. The ideological distance between Iranian conservatives and reform- ers is responsible for these groups’ different views of the United States. Chapter 3 assesses the Syrian-Iranian alliance. While this alliance has often been described as a triumph of realpolitik over ideology, Haas contends that the major sources of this alliance, in the post cold war era, have actually been ideological. Iraq’s attack on Iran, in 1980, presented an immediate and major common threat to the security of both nations, but the most important elements underlying the Syrian- Iranian alliance were the shared and intense ideological hostility toward Israel, and the ideological hardline policies by the United States in the early years of 2000. Chapter 4 examines the effects of ideological variables on Turkish foreign policy. It is argued that the internal dynamics among the main ideological groups in Turkey – Kemalists, conservatives, Islamists, and nationalists – very much shaped Turkey’s relations with Iran, Israel, the EU, and the United States. Variation in ideological 600 Book Reviews © The author(s) 2014. Nations and Nationalism © ASEN/John Wiley & Sons Ltd 2014

distance and ideological polarity were central to Turkish policymakers’ perceptions of threats to both their domestic and international interests, and thus ultimately to choices of international allies and enemies. Finally, chapter 5 considers if ideology effected Saudi-American relations. The book’s ideological argument cannot convincingly explain the post-cold war Saudi- American alliance. Haas acknowledges that material and security interests were pivotal for this alliance, despite the large ideological differences. This case is important because it uncovers the limits of ideological explanations in international relations, and the conditions under which realist theories are likely to be more accurate. In light of this ideological argument, the empirical evidence reveals three patters. First, Islamist groups consistently assumed the worst about America’s intentions in the region. Second, liberals/reformers were for the most part much more supportive of the United States, and frequently supported economic, cultural, and military cooperation with America. Finally, the policies of secular authoritarians towards America were largely in between of those of Islamists and liberalisers/reformers. These patters gen- erate key implications for America’s Middle East relations. As the book proposes, the spread of liberalism in the region is vital to America’s security, but the task involves trade-offs, and the trade-offs must be evaluated on a case-by-case basis. The Clash of Ideologies is splendidly researched and I highly recommend this masterpiece to anyone interested in security studies, international relations of Middle East, and how ideologies shape relations between nations. PERPARIM GUTAJ University of Utah Barbier, Jean-Claude, The Road to Social Europe: A Contemporary Approach to Politi- cal Cultures and Diversity in Europe. London/New York: Routledge, 2013, 220pp. £76.00 (hbk). The French sociologist Jean-Clause Barbier has written an important book on ‘Social Europe’ that is relevant to all scholars and policy makers interested in the building of Social Europe. The study is a well-elaborated, interdisciplinary approach that also offers a remedy for the restart of Social Europe. The author’s main claim is that Social Europe becomes only possible when Europe respects and promotes genuine multilin- gualism and cultural exchange among its different national communities. A precondi- tion for any restart is however a clariﬁcation and deﬁnition of theoretical key concepts such as ‘political culture’ that allow comparative research in the ﬁeld of cultural and linguistic diversity in Europe. Social sciences have ignored diversity so far. According to Barbier, this ‘blind spot’ of the social sciences is due to one-sided, standardised universalist research paradigms putting aside diversity as something of an archaic, nationalist burden of the past. Barbier convincingly demonstrates however that a comparative method is needed to determine: what is universal, what is common, and what is singular. The variable of his research paradigm is ‘national political culture’ consisting of common meanings for the linguistic identiﬁcations of values, norms, images, formal institutions, and practices rooted within a national political community. Modern social protection is more than just a set of social services. It now constitutes a genuine social relation closely interwoven with the wage-earner status of the majority Book Reviews 601 © The author(s) 2014. (9). This strongly supports the idea to lift the social protection system to the suprana- tional level of the Union. According to Barbier, a further federalisation of the Euro- pean Union is especially urgent in times of crisis in order to guarantee solidarity with the victims to ‘conserve man and nature as well as productive organization’ (13). Barbier rightly observes however that in the present Union this is not possible due to the fact that the social protection system is organised at the level of the nation state. This tension poses the central challenge of this book. The national level is characterised by cultural and linguistic diversity that makes the conceiving and legitimising of solidarity beyond borders impossible. Barbier notes that the terminology associated with the institutions, practices and values of Social Europe are profoundly linked to the terms given in the national language. Within one and the same language the meanings related to the social protection system constitute a seman- tic ‘ﬁeld’ which does not fully match a related ﬁeld in an other language. English (British) ‘social security apparatus’ does not mean precisely the same as its French counterpart ‘sécurité sociale’ and these words differ in meaning from the Danish counterpart ‘social tryghed og balance’ (social security as well as social trust and balance), and so on (107). Hence, Barbier concludes that every society is a relatively closed world with its own extended repertory of values expressed in political discourse combining a ‘collective imaginary’ with language and political activity (105). Even globalised ideas and con- cepts are reinterpreted locally generating different meanings. We only know what is at stake in other societies by translation. But translation with a pivot language for which nowadays ‘International English’ is used will not render the correct meanings of related key words in other languages. In order to understand fully the meanings in different languages the key words must be contextualised and compared (110). This book offers several theoretical, methodological and empirical innovations for which the author should be given credit. Firstly, Barbier has clearly demonstrated that the introduction of a theoretical notion like ‘political culture’ is relevant for grasping the complex nature of politics and social reality in a diverse Europe. Second, his study puts ‘diversity in Europe’ as an incorrectly neglected topic on the research agenda in social sciences. Due to an enormous amount of empirical data to be analysed, i.e. at least in the 23 ofﬁcial languages of the Union, this task can only be done by an international consortium, including experts from different scientiﬁc disciplines like social and political sciences, humanities, anthropology, economy and international studies. Third, the study offers a program for the restart of Social Europe. To overcome the different political cultures and social inequalities the language of true genuine politics cannot be unique. It has to be a plural idiom and multilingual and transnational communication skills should be included (153). Relevant skills in this context are lingua receptiva, global and regional lingua francas and code-switching (see for further dis- cussion the papers in: Normann Jørgensen, Jens (ed.), A Toolkit for Transnational Communication in Europe, Copenhagen Studies in Bilingualism, vol. 64, 2011). This will equip European citizens with tools to bridge cultures. Such policy requires however the sharing of cultures and languages and making them accessible to the masses of Europe and not for the elite only. Hence, the author concludes teaching of languages, history and humanities on a much broader scale should be promoted in Europe.
